statement: For a vector-valued function of several variables f: R^n -> R^m, f(x) = (f_1(x),...,f_m(x)) with x = (x_1,...,x_n), the Jacobian matrix J_f(x) is the m x n matrix of all first-order partial derivatives: (J_f)_{ij} = ∂f_i/∂x_j. If m = n (the matrix is square), its determinant is called the Jacobian determinant.

symbols.meaning: vector-valued function of several variables, f: R^n -> R^m
Jacobian matrix of f at x, entries (J_f)_{ij} = ∂f_i/∂x_j
point at which the Jacobian is evaluated

properties.property: The Jacobian matrix is the natural generalization of the derivative and differential of a scalar function to vector-valued functions of several variables.
properties.why: it collects all first-order partial derivatives of every component of f with respect to every input variable into one matrix

properties.property: The Jacobian matrix need not be square; it has shape m x n where m is the number of output components and n the number of inputs (e.g. Example 4: F: R^3 -> R^4 gives a 4x3 Jacobian).
properties.why: the matrix is defined by stacking ∂f_i/∂x_j for i=1..m, j=1..n, independent of whether m equals n

properties.property: When m = n, the determinant of J_f is called the Jacobian determinant, and it governs local invertibility: if J_f is continuous and nonsingular (det ≠ 0) at p, then f is invertible on some neighbourhood of p.
properties.why: this is the inverse function theorem statement given directly for the Jacobian

properties.property: If f: R^n -> R^n is invertible, the Jacobian of the inverse function satisfies J_{f^{-1}}(p) = J_f(f^{-1}(p))^{-1}, and det(J_{f^{-1}}(p)) = 1 / det(J_f(f^{-1}(p))).
properties.why: stated as the Jacobian-matrix form of the inverse function theorem

properties.property: A critical point of f: R^n -> R^m is a point where the rank of J_f is not maximal; when m = n = k, this is equivalent to the Jacobian determinant being zero at that point.
properties.why: rank deficiency of the Jacobian is the defining condition for criticality, with the square case reducing to a determinant test

properties.property: The Jacobian determinant is the local volume-scaling factor used to change variables in multiple integrals, e.g. ∬_{F(A)} f dx dy = ∬_A f(F(r,φ)) r dr dφ for polar coordinates, and the analogous ρ² sin φ factor for spherical coordinates.
properties.why: shown directly via the polar and spherical coordinate transformation examples

properties.property: For a dynamical system ẋ = F(x) with stationary point x_0 (F(x_0)=0), the eigenvalues of the Jacobian J_F(x_0) determine local stability: all eigenvalues with negative real part ⇒ stable; any eigenvalue with positive real part ⇒ unstable.
properties.why: this is the Hartman–Grobman-based stability criterion stated for the Jacobian at a stationary point

properties.property: The Jacobian matrix of a system of nonlinear equations is used by Newton's method to iteratively solve the (square) system, and serves as the linearized design matrix in nonlinear least squares / regression.
properties.why: stated as direct applications of the Jacobian

assumptions.assumption: f is differentiable, i.e. all first-order partial derivatives ∂f_i/∂x_j exist at the point of evaluation.
assumptions.breaks_when: f is not differentiable there, so the Jacobian matrix is undefined at that point

failure_modes.mode: Local invertibility fails to be guaranteed
failure_modes.signature: Jacobian determinant is zero (square case) or Jacobian is singular/not continuous at p
failure_modes.cause: the inverse function theorem's nonsingularity condition is not met, so f need not be locally invertible near p

failure_modes.mode: Stability of a stationary point cannot be determined from the Jacobian
failure_modes.signature: the largest real part among the eigenvalues of J_F(x_0) is exactly zero
failure_modes.cause: per the stated Hartman–Grobman-based criterion, this borderline case gives no conclusion about stability from the Jacobian's eigenvalues

instantiation.why_here: In agrios_ws, the ekf_global and ekf_local nodes use Extended Kalman Filters from robot_localization to fuse odometry and IMU measurements for state estimation. Because the robot's 3D kinematic motion model is non-linear, the EKF algorithm requires the Jacobian matrix to linearize the dynamics around the current state estimate and propagate covariance. This mathematical connection is strictly algorithmic within robot_localization, rather than being set by any configuration parameter.

concrete.in_your_project: The non-linear state transition function (kinematic motion model) in robot_localization that projects the robot state to the next time step (R^15 -> R^15)
The 15-dimensional robot state vector containing position, orientation, linear velocity, angular velocity, and linear acceleration (15 x 1)
The i-th scalar kinematic equation of the state transition function f that updates the i-th state variable (scalar)
The 15 x 15 state transition Jacobian matrix (F) of partial derivatives ∂f_i/∂x_j evaluated to linearize system dynamics and project covariance (15 x 15)
The number of state variables in robot_localization's state representation, which is 15 (scalar)
The number of output components of the state transition model f, which is 15 (scalar)
The current state estimate vector at which the Jacobian matrix is evaluated during the EKF prediction step (15 x 1)
